33.0.0.en: As a result of Manasseh and his people being immersed in the worship of idols and base lusts, they did not listen to the voice of God, which came by the mouth of the prophets, such as Isaiah.

33.0.1.en: This shows God's love and concern for sinners, however deeply they are immersed in sin, for He seeks the salvation of all.

33.0.2.en: Be sure that God loves you and seeks your salvation however far you have gone from Him, but may you respond to His call and return to Him quickly, whatever your sins, for He will forgive you.

33.1.0.en: Hook: a ring of bronze placed in the nose of slaves or animals, as a sign of their being owned and subject to their master.

33.1.1.en: God allowed the Assyrians, who ruled the world at that time, to attack the kingdom of Judah and seize King Manasseh, put a hook in his nose like slaves and animals, and bind him with chains, perhaps because of an accusation brought against him of rebelling against the king of Assyria. They took him to Babylon, which was at that time a city under the authority of the king of Assyria.

33.2.0.en: When Manasseh was greatly distressed and in deep humiliation in the prison of Babylon, being treated like a slave, he came to himself and felt his sins that had caused him all this humiliation, and offered repentance with contrition before God and prayed a deep prayer that the Church reads on the night of Abu Ghalamsis, that is, the Saturday of Joy. It is part of the Holy Bible that was removed from it, but the Church acknowledges it and reads it in its prayers.

33.2.1.en: And when he repented, God forgave him his sins and restored him to his kingdom in Jerusalem.

33.2.2.en: The Second Book of Kings did not mention the imprisonment of Manasseh and his prayer, nor his return from Babylon and his reforms, because when he repented he was not able to change the corruption that had spread among the people because of his many evils, and the Book of Kings is concerned with the condition of the people, whereas the Book of Chronicles is concerned with the kings as types of Christ and focuses on the good works they did more than on their evils.

33.2.3.en: The Prayer of Manasseh (this text is taken from the book of the prayers of Holy Week of the Coptic Orthodox Church) 1 O Lord Almighty, who is in heaven, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and of their seed. 2 Who made heaven and earth and all their adornment. 3 Who bound the sea by the word of Your command and sealed its depths with Your fearful name, full of glory, at which everything fears and trembles before the face of Your power. 4 For the greatness of Your glory cannot be measured. 5 And the wrath of Your anger against sinners cannot be withstood. 6 And the mercy of Your will cannot be counted or comprehended; You are the Lord Most High, merciful, long-suffering and abundant in mercy, righteous, and repenting of the evil of men. 7 You also, O Lord, according to Your goodness, have appointed repentance for him who has sinned against You. 8 And in the multitude of Your mercy You have proclaimed repentance to sinners for their salvation. 9 You, O Lord, God of the righteous, did not appoint repentance for the just, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who did not sin against You, but You appointed repentance for me, the sinner. 10 For I have sinned more than the number of the sand of the sea. 11 My iniquities are multiplied, and I am not worthy to lift up my eyes to heaven because of the multitude of my unrighteousness. 12 But I bow down because of the multitude of my iron bonds, and I cannot lift up my head because of my sins. 13 And now in truth I have provoked You, and there is no rest for me, for I have angered Your wrath; I have done evil in Your hands, and I have not done Your will, nor kept Your commandments, but I have set up my abominations and multiplied my defilements. 14 And now I bend the knees of my heart and ask of Your goodness: I have sinned, O Lord, I have sinned, and my iniquities I know. But I ask and beseech You, O Lord, forgive me, and do not destroy me with my iniquities, nor be angry with me forever, nor hold my evils against me, nor cast me into judgment in the depth beneath the earth. 15 For You are the God of those who repent. 16 And in me show Your goodness, for I am unworthy. 17 And save me according to the multitude of Your mercy, and I will praise You continually all the days of my life. 18 For You are the One to whom all the powers of the heavens sing. 19 To You is the glory forever, Amen.

33.2.4.en: The Prayer of Manasseh (this text is taken from the book of the prayers of Holy Week of the Coptic Orthodox Church) This prayer is acknowledged by the Orthodox and Catholic Churches, and it is a prayer known since the Apostolic age and found in the Septuagint translation of the books of the Old Testament, and the Coptic Orthodox Church reads it among the prayers selected from the Holy Bible on the night of the Saturday of Joy after Great Friday. This prayer appeared in the Latin Vulgate of the Holy Bible after the Second Book of Chronicles, and was also found in the Alexandrian manuscript of the Holy Bible preserved in the British Museum, and it also appeared in the Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Coptic and Ethiopic copies and all the copies taken from the Greek copy. It is a wonderful prayer of repentance that Manasseh offered to God after a long wicked life in which he led his people to the worship of idols and every evil. After it God allowed him to be taken captive to Babylon and thrown into prison, and in the humiliation of the fetters Manasseh returned to himself and offered this prayer. It is suitable for every person who repents of his sins, to encourage him and give him hope for a new life. We have given the text of the prayer, and its explanation follows.

33.3.0.en: Manasseh begins his prayer by contemplating the attributes of God and His greatness, because when a person knows God he feels His holiness and becomes small before Him, and thus he begins to feel the fear of God, which leads him to repentance. In this verse Manasseh sees in God three attributes:

33.3.1.en: 1- Almighty: in whose hand is everything and under whose authority are all human souls, Manasseh among them, and this consequently leads him to submit before God and repent of his sins. No one can flee from God, because everything is uncovered and laid bare before Him, and indeed is under His authority, and He can give him life or end it.

33.3.2.en: 2- Who is in heaven: for He is exalted above all material and earthly things, and before His exaltation the hideousness of sin appears, so a person hastens to repentance to be rid of it, and then he can stand and appear before God.

33.3.3.en: 3- God of our fathers: Manasseh has boldness with God because He is the God of his fathers. Although He is the God of the fathers and their holy seed, He also loves all the seed from whom Manasseh came and desires their salvation, which gives hope to the sinner, so that he may come forward with repentance, asking for divine forgiveness.

33.4.0.en: The fourth attribute for which Manasseh glorifies God is that He is the Creator of everything, heaven and earth and all that is in them. He adorned heaven not only with the stars and planets but rather with the angels, and He adorned the earth not only with trees, plants and animals but above all with man, for whose sake He created everything. He loves him, and therefore rejoices in his repentance and his return to Him.

33.5.0.en: In this verse Manasseh sees three other new attributes in God, besides the four previous attributes, and they are:

33.5.2.en: Despite the greatness of the seas, which with their high waves can overturn the largest ships, God set for them a law, the law of the tides, by which the waves cannot cover the dry land; rather, when the water approaches the shore it returns again to the depths. The sea resembles a mighty man bound with chains; even if it moves toward the land and what is upon it, God stops it and returns it to its place. All this develops the fear of God within a person so that he repents.

33.5.3.en: 6- He sealed the depths of the sea: Although man has gone down into the sea and learned much about it, he is still unable to reach all the depths of the seas, does not know the creatures that are in them, and cannot bear the conditions there. This shows the greatness of God's knowledge, of which man tries to discover something. So a person feels the weakness of his understanding before God and becomes very small, and all pride leaves him.

33.5.5.en: If God moves the sea with His hand as though it were a small plaything, then everything in heaven and on earth is terrified before His power. When whirlwinds and hurricanes blow, they uproot huge trees and buildings before them and stir the seas so that they overflow onto the land. When the mountains move by earthquakes, and the icebergs by heat, and everything is terrified before the power of God, a person feels his weakness and at the same time trusts in the power of God that protects him, so he takes refuge in the arms of God with repentance and contrition.

33.6.0.en: In this verse he sees a new attribute in God, which is:

33.6.1.en: 8- Unlimited: the glory of God that appears in nature in different forms surpasses the mind of man, and it is hard for him to know everything about it, which dazzles a person, so he humbles himself before God and keeps contemplating His beauty all the days, because He is unlimited.

33.7.0.en: And Manasseh sees a new attribute that concerns man directly, which is:

33.7.1.en: 9- The wrath of His anger: the great, righteous and holy God is all light and is repelled by any evil; rather, He is greatly angry with sinners who persist in their evil, and this increases the fear of God in a person's heart, which pushes him to repentance.

33.7.2.en: Contemplate the attributes of God so that your heart is drawn to Him, and you praise Him and glorify Him, and this pushes you to purity and the rejection of every sin.

33.8.s.en: (2) The God of those who repent

33.8.0.en: As he contemplates the attributes of God, Manasseh moves in his prayer to God's love for mankind, His mercy and His forgiveness of their sins, and he sees in Him the following:

33.8.1.en: 1- His unlimited mercy: besides His justice, His wrath and His severe punishment of sinners who persist in their evils, He is also very merciful to all repentant sinners; indeed, His mercy cannot be counted. Whatever the sins of Manasseh and however wide his evils, the mercy of God is wider, because it is unlimited and forgives all the sins of the repentant.

33.8.2.en: 2- Most High, merciful: although God is very high and exalted above all men, He is very tender, for He sees men as His children, so He forgives them their sins of which they repent.

33.8.3.en: 3- Long-suffering: God was long-suffering toward Manasseh for decades of years and did not end his life, to give him an opportunity to repent, and finally, when he entered into affliction during his imprisonment in Babylon, he repented, so he obtained God's mercies in this prayer.

33.8.4.en: 4- Righteous, and repenting of evil: God is holy, but He hates evil and does not desire the punishment of His children, because He "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth" (1 Tim 2:4). God's repenting here of punishing the wicked means His turning back from punishing them when they repent, as He did with the people of Nineveh.

33.9.0.en: Then Manasseh sees a new attribute in God toward His repentant children, which is:

33.9.2.en: which appeared in His readiness to forgive all the sins of His children, and He set the way to that, which is repentance.

33.10.0.en: Finally Manasseh glorifies God, who receives the worst of sinners, and says to Him: Even though You ascribe Yourself to the righteous fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob because You are righteous and holy, yet when You set repentance You did not intend it for the righteous, but for wicked sinners like me, Manasseh, who did many evils before You.

33.10.1.en: How beautiful is repentance! It is the great way that carries the worst of sinners into the arms of God, so hasten to it whatever your sins, that you may enjoy His divine love.

33.11.0.en: With contrition Manasseh confesses that his sins are very many and were repeated in a way he cannot count, so that he says they are more than the number of the sand of the sea, and this shows two things:

33.11.1.en: 1- Manasseh persisted for decades in spreading the worship of idols and all the lusts and evils that accompany it.

33.11.2.en: 2- His intense regret for these sins and his feeling of the multitude of his sins.

33.12.0.en: Because of the multitude of his sins Manasseh feels deep contrition, so he looks to the earth, that is, to the dust from which he was taken, because Adam his father was created from the dust. And he feels he is not worthy to lift his eyes toward God in heaven. Although he longs for the pure heavenly life, in humility he declares that in himself he is unworthy of it. It is God who will grant him forgiveness as a free grace, so that he may be able to look at Him. His sense of regret is increased by the fact that he wronged many, not only by taking their rights but by causing them to stumble, because he led his people astray from the worship of God and encouraged them to idolatry and every evil in it (2 Kgs 21:9). His injustice reached those nearest to him, for he killed his son, offering him as a sacrifice to Molech and burning him with fire to please this pagan god (2 Kgs 21:6). In sum, he shed much blood unjustly (2 Kgs 21:16).

33.13.0.en: His sins make Manasseh bow his head toward the earth, not only because of the weight of the iron fetters with which his hands were bound, but even more because of the hideousness of his sins, which he carried on his back, so he bowed down to the earth weeping and broken, that God might not deprive him but forgive him.

33.14.0.en: I have angered Your wrath: I have stirred up Your intense anger against me and deserved every punishment.

33.14.1.en: My abominations: my defiled and filthy evils.

33.14.2.en: Manasseh declares his responsibility for stirring up God's anger against him because of the multitude of his sins. This made him troubled, having lost his peace and rest. And when Manasseh repented, he discovered that his sins were uncovered before God, and that in ignorance he had done all these evils in God's hands. Even though God had been long-suffering toward him, he deserved discipline and every punishment.

33.14.3.en: Manasseh also declares his responsibility for rejecting God's commandments and will, since he did the opposite, which are sins and all kinds of uncleanness and defilement. In defiance of God, Manasseh set up idols and pagan worship in every place of his kingdom, even before the Temple of God itself, and now he confesses that all these were very hideous sins.

33.14.4.en: If you offer repentance for your sins and show their hideousness, you draw God's mercies upon you and enjoy His mercy, but if you neglect repentance you bring God's wrath upon yourself, so take care to examine yourself every day, that you may sleep at peace in the hands of God.

33.15.s.en: (4) Manasseh's humility and his asking for forgiveness

33.15.0.en: Be angry with me forever: that is, You would cast me into eternal torment as a punishment for my sins.

33.15.1.en: Finally, in humility which he expresses not only by bending his knees but the knees of his heart, that is, Manasseh is broken, and from this humility he looks to the goodness of God, asking forgiveness of his sins. He is unworthy because of the multitude of his sins, but his hope is in the mercy of God. As he confesses and affirms his sins and his knowledge of his evils, he implores God to forgive him all these sins and not to call him to account for them, or be angry with him and bear a grudge against him because of these evils, and so cast him into eternal destruction.

33.16.0.en: Manasseh describes God with a beautiful attribute, that He is the God of those who repent. There is no person without sin, but there is one who returns by repentance, and he is one of the children of God, and there is one who insists on his sins, and he is one of the children of the devil.

33.17.0.en: Manasseh begs God to show His goodness in him, that is, His mercy; for despite Manasseh's unworthiness he begs God to grant him forgiveness as a divine grace. And he hopes that God will give him of His goodness, that is, make Manasseh good.

33.18.0.en: When Manasseh receives salvation from his many sins and forgiveness through the multitude of God's mercies, this pushes him to praise God and glorify Him all the days of his life. For the divine forgiveness of all these sins surpasses the mind, and Manasseh has nothing but thanksgiving and praise. This is the feeling of every truly repentant person before God.

33.19.0.en: Thus Manasseh joins the angels, who are the powers and hosts of heaven, and praises God with them; that is, Manasseh does his natural work as a man, beginning with praise on earth, which is completed in heaven after his departure from this body.

33.19.1.en: It is clear that a person immersed in sin has no spiritual inclinations, so he does not love prayer and praise, but when his sins are released, his feelings are set free for prayer and praise.

33.19.2.en: Thank God every day after you confess your sins, because He receives you and forgives them to you, and awaits you in the sacraments of Confession and Communion, to complete His grace for you. Indeed, hold fast to your prayers and your praises every day, because they are your natural life and your delight.

33.20.0.en: The City of David: also called Mount Zion, located in the southeast of Jerusalem, and in it are the tombs of the kings of Judah.

33.20.1.en: Gihon: it is the Kidron Valley, which extends from the northeast of the city of Jerusalem to its south. The Fish Gate: one of the gates of Jerusalem, located in its north and beside the fish market, through which the fishermen enter with their fish.

33.20.2.en: Ophel: a fortified high place located east of Jerusalem, south of the Temple and north of the City of David, or Mount Zion.

33.20.3.en: After Manasseh's repentance he cared for the kingdom of Judah and began with Jerusalem, so he built a wall for it, extending from the north of the city at the Fish Gate and turning westward until it reached the south of the city, at the Kidron Valley. He also built a very high wall around Ophel, which is a very fortified place.

33.20.4.en: He also cared for the protection of the cities of Judah and placed in each of them one of the commanders of his army, with a large number of soldiers.

33.20.5.en: This signifies that the repentant person should fortify himself against the attacks of evil, and not be satisfied with rejecting sin but strengthen his relationship with God, so that the devil cannot attack him or overcome him.

33.20.6.en: Hold fast to your spiritual striving throughout your life, and do not be satisfied with leaving the difficult sins into which you have often fallen, but be constant in your relationship with God, growing in His fear and love.

33.21.0.en: The images: statues resembling the gods; it is said that Manasseh also made statues of himself resembling him, for them to worship.

33.21.1.en: The mountain of the house of the Lord: a hill located northeast of the city of Jerusalem, called Mount Moriah.

33.21.2.en: Among the important works that King Manasseh did after his repentance was removing the idols and the altars of the idols that he had built in Jerusalem, and even inside the two courts of the house of the Lord (v. 5), and he cast these statues outside Jerusalem, but unfortunately he did not break them or burn them, as other righteous kings did. Therefore, when his son Amon reigned after him, he took these statues and set them up again, worshipped them and sacrificed (v. 22).

33.22.0.en: Manasseh removed the pagan worship that he had set up in the days of his early reign, when he was far from God before he repented, a period of nearly fifty years; for he reigned fifty-five years, and he began to reign at the age of twelve and was taken captive at the age of fifty-eight (in the year 648 B.C.), as the ancient manuscripts indicate; that is, he repented in the last years of his life, after his return from Babylon.

33.22.1.en: After he repented, Manasseh cared not only about removing the pagan worship but also about calling his people to the worship of God; for he repaired the altar of God, which had been neglected for decades of years, then offered upon it peace offerings and thanksgiving to God, who accepted his repentance, and he encouraged his people, indeed commanded them to worship God as He commanded in His law.

33.23.0.en: Manasseh removed the temples of the idols and the statues, but time did not allow him to remove the high places on which they offered worship to the host of heaven. But Manasseh forbade offering any pagan worship upon them, so the people offered upon them the worship of God and sacrifices, though this was not right, because sacrifices should be offered only in the Temple of God; yet at least this worship was a return to God and a rejection of the idols.

33.24.0.en: The seers: plural of seer, a person who sees visions from God and prophesies and proclaims the voice of God to the people, and who wrote the visions, prophecies and instructions in a book.

33.24.1.en: As for the details of Manasseh's life, whether in the period of his evil conduct and his encouragement of the worship of idols by which he led the people astray from God, all of it is written in the acts of the kings of Israel and also the acts of the seers. In these books the seers' rebuke of Manasseh in the days of his departure from God is mentioned, and then these books contain his repentance and his return to God, then his prayer, which God answered, so He brought him back from Babylon, and he began his reforms in Jerusalem and Judea, as evidence of his repentance and his attempt to bring the people back to God, although only a few of them returned, because they had become fixed in the worship of idols and had forgotten God.

33.25.0.en: Manasseh died after he had reigned 55 years, at the age of 67, and it seems that he commanded that they bury him in the garden of his house, because he felt he was unworthy to be buried in the tombs of the kings, and this shows his humility and his deep repentance. Then his son Amon reigned after him.

33.26.s.en: (4) The reign of Amon over Judah

33.26.0.en: After the death of Manasseh his son Amon reigned, and he was twenty-two years old, that is, a young man, and he was the fifteenth king on the throne of Judah. He walked in evil, offered sacrifices to the idols and departed from God, and did not learn from the repentance of his father, which took place when he entered into great affliction in his imprisonment in Babylon.

33.26.1.en: May you learn from the virtues of others and also from their mistakes, so that you try to acquire the virtues and keep away from the mistakes whose bitter end you have seen. Everything that happens around you is a personal message to you from God, that you may turn away from your sins and draw near to Him.

33.27.0.en: Amon continued in evil and the worship of idols and did not return from them by repentance to God like his father; perhaps he said, I will repent later, as my father repented, but I want to enjoy lusts now, and he forgot that he does not know the day of his end in this world. So he reigned only two years, and this was by God's arrangement, so that he would not increase his evils and draw his people further away from God.

33.27.1.en: Most likely the people continued in the worship of idols and did not repent with Manasseh, which helped Amon in the worship of idols, perhaps by the encouragement of his counselors and servants. In general, this shows us that the evil a person does causes others to stumble, and even if he repents he may not be able to bring back to God those whom he caused to stumble.

33.28.0.en: God ended the life of Amon two years after he became king, when he was twenty-four years old, for his servants rose up against him and killed him, and so his evil came upon his own head.

33.29.0.en: The people of the kingdom of Judah were enraged at the killers of the king, so they killed them. They buried Amon in the garden of his house, which is called the garden of Uzza (2 Kgs 21:26). Then they made his young child Josiah king after him. Josiah the righteous king
